blocks.text: Reflect , by artist Cannupa Hanska Luger , is the second exhibition presented by For Freedoms at the Corcoran School of the Arts and Design .

Reflect is a living archive of Cannupa Hanska Luger’s Mirror Shield Project , marking ten years since its creation. Rooted in Northern Plains Indigenous traditions, “counting coup” describes an act of courage defined not by violence but by approaching an adversary closely enough to recognize their humanity without causing harm. Luger utilizes this principle as an artistic methodology grounded in proximity, accountability, restraint, and recognition, one that runs throughout Counting Coup: We Are the People , his broader residency encompassing exhibitions, public programs, and community activities.

“Ten years since the creation of a mirror shield and the concept remains relevant. My personal thoughts are that someday it will be forgotten and the need for such devices will become unfathomable,” says Cannupa Hanska Luger.

The Mirror Shield Project was initiated by Luger (Mandan, Hidatsa, Arikara, Lakota) in 2016 in support of the Water Protectors at Očhéthi Šakówiŋ (Oceti Sakowin) Camp near Standing Rock, North Dakota. Luger, who grew up on the Standing Rock Reservation, developed the project as an artistic response and a way to mobilize creative communities in solidarity with Indigenous sovereignty and the protection of land and water.

Designed from lightweight, inexpensive, readily available materials, the shields were intentionally easy to reproduce. While an Artist-in-Residence at the Institute of American Indian Arts, Luger worked with Oglala Lakota/Diné filmmaker Razelle Benally to create How to Build Mirror Shields for Water Protectors , an instructional film shared openly through social media. Within weeks, artists, activists, students, families, and anonymous community members across the country created and transported upwards of a thousand mirrored shields to Očhéthi Šakówiŋ Camp, while Water Protectors made additional shields onsite.

From the beginning, Luger imagined the mirrored surfaces not only as a form of protection, but as a way to turn the gaze of surveillance back upon itself. Working with artist Rory Erler Wakemup (Minnesota Chippewa Tribe) and the Water Protector community at Očhéthi Šakówiŋ, hundreds of shields were brought together in a large-scale action in which Water Protectors moved through the camp holding mirrors overhead, their bodies forming a river. The reflective surfaces were turned skyward toward the police surveillance aircraft continually circling above the camp, returning the apparatus of surveillance back onto those watching from above. In other frontline actions, the mirrors reflected the militarized police back to themselves, attempting to interrupt the abstraction of conflict and reveal the human being behind the uniform.

The Mirror Shield Project emerged from a much larger movement of Indigenous liberation already underway at Standing Rock. The resistance to the Dakota Access Pipeline was not simply an environmental campaign, but an assertion of Indigenous sovereignty, relationship, and responsibility to land, water, and future generations. The Mirror Shield Project became Luger’s contribution to that larger movement: an artwork conceived not simply to represent resistance, but to become useful within it. A humble act of making in one place could become an act of solidarity somewhere else.

In the decade since Standing Rock, the project has continued to move between frontline action, Indigenous land and water defense, community making, performance, exhibition, and scholarship. Because the design was released as open source by the artist, its history belongs not to a single author, but to the many hands and communities that have carried it forward. Mirrored shields have appeared in Stop Line 3 actions opposing the Enbridge Line 3 pipeline, in Black Lives Matter actions across the United States, and anonymously in resistance movements around the world. In many of its museum presentations, the project has remained active rather than archival, inviting communities to make and activate new shields locally and allowing the work to move beyond exhibition spaces and back into community and social action.

At the Corcoran, Reflect celebrates this ten-year lineage while carrying the engagement ethos of the Mirror Shield Project forward. The exhibition functions as both a living archive and a working toolshed. Visitors, artists, students, and community groups are invited not only to encounter the history of the project, but to participate in its continued life through social collaboration, shield-making, and performance activation.

Ten years after Standing Rock, the full reach of the Mirror Shield Project remains impossible to trace — and that is precisely its legacy. The larger movement for Indigenous liberation continues to take new forms: asserting sovereignty, defending land and water, strengthening relationships, and imagining futures beyond colonial systems. Within the larger living Indigenous liberation movement, the Mirror Shield Project continues in motion, carried forward not through ownership, but through participation.
On view at the Corcoran October 28, 2026 – February 19, 2027
